bullets: Two giant plates of rock drift towards each other, collide, and one slides underneath the other
slides.heading: Plate tectonics: giant slabs on the move
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we meet plate tectonics - the giant slabs of rock that make up the Earth's crust - starting with two plates sitting apart, then pushing together, one sliding under the other, and finally how slowly they really move.

bullets: Name the giant slabs that make up the Earth's crust and say what they do
Explain what happens when two plates push together and what subduction means
Say how fast plates really move and why they move that way
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to name the plates, explain subduction, and give the true speed of plate movement.

bullets: A pupil pictures the plates moving in sudden jumps from one position to the next
Is that how plates really travel, or is the true movement far slower and steadier?
slides.heading: Do plates jump or creep?
slides.notes: Pose the sudden-jump picture without the verdict first: ask for a show of hands on whether plates jump suddenly or creep steadily, take two or three answers without judging them, and say scene s4 settles this exactly.

bullets: The Earth's crust is made of giant slabs of rock called plates
Year after year the plates drift, push together, and sometimes one slides under another
Plates move only about two centimetres a year - slower than your fingernails grow
slides.heading: The crust is made of giant moving slabs
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: the ground under our feet is not one solid piece - it is giant plates that drift, collide and sink, all at a creeping pace no one can feel.

bullets: Plate A and Plate B are two giant slabs of the Earth's crust
Year after year, the plates drift towards each other
slides.heading: Two giant plates of rock sit apart
slides.notes: Narrate the two plates as they appear in the animation: point to Plate A and Plate B sitting apart, then watch them begin to drift towards each other - the labels name the slabs, drift names the slow movement.

bullets: The drift becomes a push as the two plates keep moving towards each other
The two plates collide head-on where they meet
slides.heading: The plates push together
slides.notes: Follow the push arrows as the plates close the gap: the slow drift becomes a head-on collision, and where they meet something has to give - watch the next scene to see which plate goes under.

bullets: Where the plates meet, the denser plate is forced down under the other
That sinking of one plate under another is called subduction
slides.heading: One plate slides under the other
slides.notes: Watch the denser plate dive below the lighter one: name the key word subduction as it sinks, and stress that the lighter plate rides on top while the denser plate slides underneath.

bullets: Real plates move only about two centimetres a year
That is slower than your fingernails grow - a steady creep, never a sudden jump
slides.heading: Plates creep, they never lurch
slides.notes: Watch the marker creep across the plate: in a whole year it travels only about two centimetres, so plates move with a steady creep that no one can feel, never with a sudden jump.

bullets: Start with the two plates sitting apart, drifting towards each other year after year
They push together and collide, the denser plate slides under in subduction, and the whole movement creeps at about two centimetres a year
slides.heading: Worked example: follow two plates from apart to sinking
slides.notes: Talk through the chain slowly and name each step: plates apart first, then the push and collision, then the denser plate sinking in subduction, and finish with the speed - a creep of about two centimetres a year.

bullets: Put the four scenes in order and say what happens at each step
Explain in one sentence how fast plates move and what subduction means
slides.heading: Your turn: trace the plates and give the speed
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them to order the scenes correctly, to use the word subduction for the sinking plate, and to give the true creeping speed.

bullets: On your own: name the giant slabs of rock that make up the crust
Say what subduction is, and how fast plates really move in a year
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the word plates, a clear meaning of subduction, and the true speed - about two centimetres a year, a creep and never a sudden jump.

subject: geography
title: Plate tectonics: giant slabs on the move
